articles.body:
The trajectory of education policy in a trio of historically red states is about to see a major shakeup after voters there elected Democratic governors for the first time in decades.

For years, positions on school choice, LGBTQ topics in classrooms and efforts either for or against diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) have expanded cultural divides between blue and red states, and now, with Democrats taking charge over a wider map, battles will be brewing in state legislatures.

That’s particularly true in Texas, Georgia, Iowa, where for years Republicans have held the governors’ mansions and backed policies that have expanded school choice , restricted books in classrooms, led to courses axed from universities and added Bible lessons to K-12 curriculum.

The governors in these states won’t have free rein, facing divided statehouses and GOP lawmakers firmly opposed to their plans, but the power to appoint individuals to state positions, veto bills and drive the legislative agenda will give huge advantages to the Democratic education platform.

While Gina Hinojosa, the Democratic governor-elect in Texas, has said little about DEI in classrooms, for example, she has regularly criticized the state’s school choice program as a giveaway to private schools. Hinojosa says she is committed to “end the voucher scam” after Gov. Greg Abbott (R) spent years fighting for government-funded accounts that students can use to leave their local public school.

While Republicans still control the Texas Senate, Hinojosa will have line-item veto power that she could use to attempt to defund the program, even if she can’t end it completely without legislative support.

And the fight could begin before she’s even sworn in.

Corey DeAngelis, a research fellow at the Heritage Foundation, said Abbott could call a special session before he leaves office “to protect school choice.”

“The current Republican Legislature can pass a bill in special session to move the program into the state school funding formula instead. That change would largely eliminate the ability to kill it with a line-item veto,” DeAngelis said.

Hinojosa will also have the ability to appoint members to Texas higher education oversight board, although her choices would need to get through a Republican Texas Senate.

But the new leadership brings hope for those who have been concerned about the decline of academic freedom in Texas.

“We’re hopeful because the folks who did get elected were folks who were very supportive of our students’ learning ability, our students’ learning, and I think this is going to be good for them,” said Teresa L. Klein, president of the American Association of University Professors-American Federation of Teachers Texas Conference. “We want to see academic freedom recognized and shared governance restored; those are things that we’ll be surely discussing with all the legislators.”

In Iowa, restrictions on LGBTQ books in schools and a universal school choice program have angered liberals who failed in court to reverse the book ban.

Unlike in Texas, Rob Sand, the Democratic governor-elect in Iowa, ran a platform to reform the state’s school choice program instead of wiping it out.

He also emphasized increased public funding and universal pre-K.

“Interestingly, in each of those states, the Democrats did not tote the traditional party line, which was to be against school choice, including they weren’t against private school choice, either. They did, in various forms, raise concerns about their state’s choice programs, but it was more in terms of how do we tweak them to better align with our values and to advance our priorities than entirely do away with it,” said Jorge Elorza, CEO of Democrats for Education Reform.

Under GOP leadership, Georgia has focused on banning “divisive concepts” in classrooms and passing a Parental Bill of Rights that allows reviews of instructional materials by parents.

Democratic Governor-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms has so far largely stayed out of the school choice conversation and focused on free universal community college, pre-K and expanding financial literacy.

She also said she would support “eliminating state income taxes for teachers.”

In an interview in 2022 when Bottoms was mayor of Atlanta, she told VOX ATL , “To not allow educators to have open discussions in their classrooms does a disservice to students across our state and can have generational repercussions because they didn’t have the benefit of understanding the racial dynamics of who we are.”

“I think we can expect Governor Elect Bottoms in Georgia to adopt more progressive measures to enhance the education funding to fully support schools. I also think that she’s ran on issues around supporting teachers … so we might see additional measures at the state level to increase teacher salaries or to provide more incentives to attract and retain high quality or high impact teachers,” said Weadé James, senior director for K-12 Education Policy at the Center for American Progress.

articles.title: Jewish teens prepare to combat antisemitism on campus with history, humor and courage
articles.summary: Jewish Student Union presidents gathered to prepare for antisemitism on college campuses, hearing from activists like Shai Davidai and Tessa Veksler.
articles.body: Jewish high school student leaders gathered for three days of fun and learning as part of the Jewish Student Union's (JSU) annual Presidents Conference. The event brought together student club presidents from across the U.S. with the goal of preparing them to combat antisemitism not only at their current high schools, but also on their future college campuses. "Jewish students have increasingly been feeling isolated, bullied, and threatened by students at their public high schools," National Conference of Synagogue Youth (NCSY) International director Rabbi Micah Greenland told Fox News Digital. "And the fact that they have JSU spaces to gather in makes those clubs all the more important as community spaces of gathering. For Jewish students and their allies." Greenland said he expected students to leave the conference with the ability to "more effectively reach out to their peers" when they return home. OPINION: BEYOND THE SUPER BOWL AD: WHY JEWISH TEENS NEED MORE THAN A MOMENT TO FIGHT ANTISEMITISM IN SCHOOLS Rabbi Derek Gormin, who serves as a managing director at JSU, explained that the organization started at a high school in California and has since grown to more than 500 clubs since its inception. He also emphasized the importance of peer-to-peer interactions, something that JSU prioritized. "Every club is run by teens. JSU has a staff internationally, but we can't show up to a school and say we'd like to start a club," Gormin told Fox News Digital. "Student to student, peer to peer, there's an unbelievable power that's created when they work together and that movement continues to grow from that peer-to-peer power." The emphasis on "peer-to-peer power" was demonstrated in real time at the conference with Hillel Kornwasser, an activist and high school student from New Jersey, serving as one of the presenters. "For me, it's a little weird. I'm getting up in front of a room with some kids my age or kids a year older than me, but the reality is there's no waiting till tomorrow for this fight," Kornwasser told Fox News Digital. Despite still being a teenager, Kornwasser is already thinking about the world in which he wants to raise his future children. He underscored that he's not the only person his age with these concerns, saying that many at the conference shared them as well. "The world that we live in today, in America, in New York City, the western world as a whole, is not a world that I want my children to — my future children to — grow up in," he said. "In a world where they have to look behind their shoulder every single second with a yarmulke on or their Star of David out wondering if the next person is going to stab them in the back literally and figuratively for being Jewish." JEWISH STUDENT TARGETED WITH ANTISEMITIC ABUSE, LAPTOP CORD ATTACK AT COLORADO SCHOOL, ADL ALLEGES JSU's conference also brought together Jewish educators from all walks of life, including activist Tessa Veksler, actor and content creator Noa Bess Solomon, author and activist Shai Davidai and Jerusalem Education Institute (JEI) founder and senior educator Charlotte Korchak. On Oct. 7, 2023, when Hamas launched its attacks in Israel, Veksler was a senior at University of California Santa Barbara (UCSB), where she served as student body president. She told Fox News Digital that, after the attacks in Israel, she was forced to bear the brunt of antisemitism at UCSB. "I went through a year of harassment, consistently both in person and online, which culminated in a recall campaign to remove me from office because I was pro-Israel and Jewish," she told Fox News Digital. When she was in high school, Veksler was involved in JSU, making the conference a full-circle moment for her. She told Fox News Digital that she hoped her presence at the conference served as a reminder to students that they "have so much more to gain than to lose" when it comes to combatting antisemitism and speaking out for Israel. However, she acknowledged that concerns about doing so were valid. "The hardest thing about being a pro-Israel student on a college campus right now is feeling like there is a target on your back. I think that it's never been scarier to be a Jewish student on a college campus," Veksler said. "We're seeing students get attacked on college campuses. We're seeing professors spewing hateful rhetoric in the classroom. It's a scary time, but also an incredible time for Jewish students to step up and pro-Israel students." In 2024, Veksler was allegedly harassed with antisemitic signs on campus, including ones that read "Tessa Veksler supports genocide" and "Zionists not welcome," according to ABC News. UCSB Chancellor Henry T. Yang released a statement following the incidents, in which he provided the community with an update on the school's "Principles of Community" memo, which was released on Oct. 26, 2023. "We were distressed to learn of incidents over the weekend that included offensive social media messages and signage at the Multicultural Center entrance. Campus offices are reviewing these unauthorized and unofficial messages," the statement signed by Yang read. "The signage has been removed and campus is conducting a bias incident review based on potential discrimination related to protected categories that include religion, citizenship, and national or ethnic origin. The posting of such messages is a violation of our principles of community and inclusion." "We strive to create opportunities for civil dialogue, free from bullying and discrimination, that allow all community members to have their voices heard, and to have a space in which to respectfully express their views," the statement continued. "To ensure that we uphold our community values and principles, the campus is committed to thoroughly reviewing and addressing all reported bias incidents." JEWISH CAMPUS LIFE AT A ‘CROSSING POINT’ AS STUDENTS WEIGH ANTISEMITISM RISKS, NEW REPORT SHOWS For Davidai, who became nationally known after speaking out about antisemitism at Columbia University, the key is to ensure that students are armed with facts and empathy. He said he was hoping to assure the JSU leaders that they would be able to speak up for themselves in college when faced with antisemitic and anti-Israel rhetoric. During one of his student sessions running mock debates, Davidai told participants to keep in mind what he called "the three E's," advising them to "engage with empathy and evidence." "I think the most important lesson that they should get is that you cannot engage just with facts," he told Fox News Digital. "You have to appeal to people's emotions, you have to acknowledge that they are humans, you have to show them a lot of empathy, and at the same time, whatever you do, the end decision needs to be based on evidence and fact." Davidai also taught students that a person's volume does not necessarily make their argument correct or worth engaging with. He said the lesson emerged from research for his book, "American Intellectual Antisemitism: The Anti-Jewish Movement Tearing Through Our Universities." Davidai said his research found that the people making the most noise on college campuses, including faculty, staff and students, represented "a minority opinion." "The problem is that they are very, very loud, they have a lot of power on campus, and they take control of the agenda," he told Fox News Digital. "And what I'm trying to teach the students here is that they can stand up to them, that when someone is being loud, that just that doesn't mean that they're being right, and it doesn't mean that they should go unopposed." CONSERVATIVE JEWISH ACTIVIST VOWS NOT TO BE SILENCED AFTER BEING ATTACKED ON UNIVERSITY OF MICHIGAN CAMPUS While Davidai focused on how students engage in tough conversations, Korchak emphasized the importance of students understanding what they were being asked to defend. "They need to know their story," Korchak told Fox News Digital. "They need to [know] how to explain to people what Jews are, why a Jewish state, why the land of Israel, right?" Korchak explained that understanding history also meant knowing how to combat false arguments. She said that JEI worked to prepare students to combat false claims about Israel and challenge them with historically accurate arguments. "When you know the history, and you know the contemporary situation, then it's so easy to have a conversation because it's not coming from a sound bite that you were taught or a one-liner, but it's coming from deep knowledge," she said. However, the conference wasn't solely focused on combating antisemitism. Solomon, an actor and content creator at Lost Tribe, was there to show students how to embrace joy and laughter. "I always say that the key to surviving as a Jewish person is being able to laugh and have humor," Solomon, who co-hosts the "What Are We" podcast, told Fox News Digital. "I think, it's like, if you don't laugh, you cry, and laughter is the best medicine." Solomon underscored her pride in being Jewish, saying she wants the students to walk away from their interactions with students embracing their Judaism and not feeling as though it's all about politics. "There's nothing political about being Jewish," Solomon said. "It's your grandma's — it's your bubbie's matzo ball soup, it's camp, it's food, it's tradition, and that's exactly what I want to keep reminding these kids." Solomon's message was reflected in the broader theme of the conference: Preparing Jewish students to confront antisemitism while ensuring that fear does not overshadow their connection to Judaism. JSU leaders said that they hope that when the students return to school, they will have the tools they need to combat antisemitism and the confidence to be openly and proudly Jewish.
